Question #1: Run 17 / 5, 17 %% 5, and 17 %/% 5 side by side. In your own words, explain how these three results relate to each other mathematically.

```{r}
17 / 5 
17 %% 5 
17 %/% 5
```
17/5 outputs 3.4 since it only divides the dividend by the divisor to provide the exact, continuous numeric value. 
17 %% 5 outputs 2 since it only calculates the leftover value (remainder) that remains after performing floored integer division. 
17 %/% 5 outputs 3 since it Divides the numbers and discards the fractional part, returning only the largest whole integer (quotient).


### Part B — Basic Data Types: typeof(), class(), and mode()
# TODO: Use typeof() to check the type of each of x, y, z, w, v
```{r}
x <- 42
y <- 42L  
z <- "42"
w <- TRUE
v <- 3 + 2i 
typeof(x)
typeof(y)
typeof(z)
typeof(w)
typeof(v)
```
# TODO: Use class() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
```{r}
class(x)
class(y)
class(z)
class(w)
class(v)
```
# TODO: Use mode() to check the class of each of x, y, z, w, v
```{r}
mode(x)
mode(y)
mode(z)
mode(w)
mode(v)
```
Question #3: x <- 42 and y <- 42L look almost identical, but typeof(x) and typeof(y) give different answers. Explain the difference in your own words.

x <- 42 creates a double decimal because R stores all numbers as decimals by default, while y <- 42L uses the L to force R to store it as an integer or whole number.

Question #4: Is typeof() ever different from class() and from mode() for the same object? Look at your results above and explain any case where this happens (or, if you did not see one, explain what you would expect for a matrix or factor).

Yes, they can differ because they look at the object from different angles:
typeof(): Identifies how R stores the data in computer memory at the lowest internal level.
class(): Identifies the object's high-level category or object-oriented class that dictates how R functions treat it.
mode(): Identifies an older S-language compatibility layer that groups types into broader categories.

Question #5: When you ran the conversion-fail chunk, R produced NA and a warning instead of stopping with an error.

Why do you think R is designed to give a warning here rather than crashing the whole script?

R keeps running to finish processing the rest of the dataset. If a list contains thousands of numbers, the entire script should not stop just because one row has a typo. R marks the typo as NA (missing) and moves on to complete the remaining tasks.

What are the risks of this behavior if you don’t read your warnings?

Final calculations can quietly become incorrect. If a text typo turns into an NA without being noticed, it ruins the mathematical operations.

Question #6: as.logical(0) and as.logical(1) convert to FALSE and TRUE.

What do you think as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1)` will produce?

Both as.logical(2) and as.logical(-1) will produce TRUE.

```{r}

as.logical(2)


as.logical(-1)

```

Test it, then explain the rule R seems to be following.

The number 0 becomes FALSE, and any non-zero number becomes TRUE. It does not matter if the number is positive, negative, or a decimal; if it is not exactly zero, R treats it as true.

```{r}

```

```{r}
print(first_name)

```
# TODO: Use paste() to combine first_name and last_name into a full name
# TODO: Use paste0() to do the same, and compare the two results

```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"
full_name_paste <- paste(first_name, last_name)
full_name_paste0 <- paste0(first_name, last_name)

full_name_paste
full_name_paste0
```

# last_name with a dash instead of a space

```{r}

paste(first_name, last_name, sep = "-")
```
# TODO: Use paste0() to build the sentence:
# "Juan Dela Cruz is 21 years old." by combining full_name, age, and text
```{r}
first_name <- "Juan"
last_name <- "Dela Cruz"
age <- 21
full_name <- paste(first_name, last_name)

paste0(full_name, " is ", age, " years old.")
```
Question #7: paste() and paste0() produced different results for the same two strings. Explain exactly why, referencing what each function does by default.

The functions use different default separators. paste() defaults to a space separator (sep = " "), adding a space between text strings. paste0() defaults to no separator (sep = ""), joining the strings directly together without spaces



Question #8: In the strings-numbers chunk, you combined a character string with a numeric variable (age) using paste0() without first converting age to a string.

Did this cause an error? Explain what paste0() does internally to make this work, and how it relates to the type conversions you practiced in Part C.

No, it did not cause an error. paste0() automatically converts the numeric age into a character string before joining it. This is implicit coercion, where R performs the same conversion as as.character() automatically behind the scenes.



Question #9: Some programming languages automatically convert "5" + 5 into 10 without an error. R does not.

Based on what you’ve learned about R’s data types in this lab, why do you think R requires an explicit conversion instead of guessing what the programmer meant?

R prioritizes data safety over guessing. Guessing can cause hidden math errors in data science. R requires explicit conversion to ensure the programmer intentionally treats text as mathematical data


Question #10: Suppose a classmate writes a script that reads a column of “numbers” from a text file. The column looks numeric, but when they try sum() on it, R throws an error. Based on everything in this lab (types, typeof()/class()/mode(), conversion, warnings), write a short paragraph explaining what likely went wrong and the steps you’d take to diagnose and fix it.

The column was likely imported as a character type instead of a numeric type. This happens when a text file contains hidden spaces, symbols, or typos. To diagnose it, use class() or typeof() to check the data type. To fix it, use as.numeric() to convert the column to numbers, and watch for any coercion warnings to find the rows causing the issue.

### Conclusion

In 3–4 sentences, summarize what you learned about how R handles different data types, and why understanding typeof()/class() and conversion functions matters before doing arithmetic or combining data.

R enforces strict rules for data types to maintain data integrity, meaning mathematical operations cannot be performed directly on character strings. Understanding functions like typeof() and class() allows programmers to verify how data is stored and avoid unexpected calculation failures. Using explicit conversion functions ensures that data is safely transformed, preventing silent data corruption and missing values. Ultimately, mastering these foundational concepts ensures that data manipulation and statistical analyses remain accurate and reliable.
